title: talent
aim: Explore how talents appear, are regretted, explained and developed through practice.
objectives: Make and read deductions about past events
Express wishes and regrets with the right structures
Explain a process in clear, ordered stages

lessons.title: An unexpected passion
goals: Understand a story about a sudden talent

grammar.title: Past modals of deduction
grammar.shortAr: must / might / can't + have + past participle للاستنتاج عن الماضي.
points: Use must have + past participle when evidence makes something almost certain.
Use might, could or may have + past participle for a possibility you are not sure about.
Use can't or couldn't have + past participle when evidence makes something impossible.
Use modal + have been + -ing or a past participle for continuous or passive deductions.
table: must have + past participle — near certainty
He must have practised for years.
might / could have + past participle — possibility
She might have had the talent as a child.
can't have + past participle — impossibility
It can't have been easy for his neighbours.
modal + have been + -ing — continuous
They can't have been living there very long.
modal + have been + past participle — passive
Her bag must have been stolen.
exceptions: For negative deductions use can't/couldn't have, not mustn't have.
In the passive, add been before the past participle.

vocab.example: His new passion was a bolt from the blue.
By chance, an old babysitter left her piano at his home.
After a freak accident, his life changed.
His interest appeared in an instant.
Something unexpected happened at the pay phone.
He was fortunate to recover fully.
He was a world-renowned surgeon.
Practising every spare moment is time-consuming.

reading.summary: An article describes how surgeon Tony Cicoria was struck by lightning and suddenly developed an intense love of classical piano. He taught himself a melody from a dream and eventually performed his own composition, The Lightning Sonata.

listening.summary: First part of the recording of the article about Tony Cicoria's sudden musical passion.
Second part of the article recording, covering his practice and first composition.
Connected-speech practice on past modals of deduction and weak forms of have.

video.summary: Speakers talk about hidden talents and abilities they would like to have.

speaking: Retell Tony Cicoria's story, adding background and specific details to make it vivid.
Speculate about how his family, neighbours and colleagues reacted, using past modals.
writing: Write a short paragraph speculating about the story with must have, might have and can't have.

practice.q: Cicoria's family ... surprised by his sudden interest.
practice.why: Strong evidence makes this almost certain.

practice.q: He ... the talent since childhood, but never knew about it.
practice.why: This is a possibility, not a certainty.

practice.q: His neighbours ... pleased about the late-night piano playing.
practice.why: A negative deduction based on strong evidence.

practice.q: His bag ... while he was in the marketplace.
practice.why: A passive deduction uses have been + past participle.

lessons.title: I wish!
goals: Talk about missed opportunities and regrets
Use wish, if only and should have correctly

grammar.title: Wish, if only and should have
grammar.shortAr: wish / if only + past simple للحاضر، + past perfect للندم، should have + past participle.
points: Use wish or if only + past simple or could for present situations you cannot change.
Use wish + object + would for annoying present behaviour; do not use it about yourself.
Use wish or if only + past perfect for past events you now regret.
Use should(n't) have + past participle to criticise or regret a past action.
table: wish + past simple — present
I wish I had more time to practise.
wish + object + would — annoyance
I wish they would be quiet at night.
if only + past perfect — strong regret
If only I'd kept going with it.
wish + past perfect — past regret
I wish I'd gone to the trial.
should(n't) have + past participle
I shouldn't have given up so early.
exceptions: If only is more emotional than wish in the same structures.
Avoid 'I wish I would...' when talking about your own behaviour.

vocab.example: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.
I thought learning Italian would be a piece of cake.
I waited too long and missed the boat.
The idea failed, so we went back to the drawing board.
Skiing was definitely not my cup of tea.

vocab.word: the grass is greener on the other side
vocab.example: I left my old job and learnt the grass is greener on the other side.
I wish I'd taken advantage of my opportunities.
He learnt the piano piece by heart.

reading.summary: Online forum posts share regrets about missed chances, easy-looking challenges and jobs left too soon. One writer explains that a disappointing result was actually a blessing in disguise.

listening.summary: Three speakers describe talents they had but did not follow, and why.
Extracts about quitting football, ignoring acting advice and leaving a band.
Chunking practice: regret idioms pronounced as single units.

speaking: Take turns discussing three personal regrets, explaining the decision, the result and how you feel now.
writing: Write a personal essay connecting a real experience to a regret idiom and explaining what you learnt.

practice.q: I wish I ... to the trial when I had the chance.
practice.why: A past regret takes wish + past perfect.

practice.q: If only I ... so careless with that opportunity!
practice.why: If only + past perfect refers to a past regret.

practice.q: I ... that job; the work was awful.
practice.why: shouldn't have + past participle criticises a past action.

practice.q: The job I turned down led me to my partner: it was ...
practice.why: The idiom means a bad event with a good outcome.

lessons.title: Let me explain
goals: Understand an article about explaining things clearly
Describe stages, necessity and warnings in a process

grammar.title: Describing a process
grammar.shortAr: To begin with / The next step / Once you've done... / It's essential / I'd recommend -ing / Avoid -ing.
points: Introduce stages in order with To begin with, The next step is to and Once you've done that.
Say what is necessary with It's essential to/that... and The final stage involves + -ing.
Say what is recommended or optional with I'd recommend + -ing, This is optional and If you want, you can...
Warn about problems with Be careful not to..., Avoid + -ing and One common mistake is to...
table: To begin with, you'll want to ...
To begin with, get your ingredients together.
The next step is to ...
The next step is to make the sauce.
Once you've done that, ...
Once you've done that, add the vegetables.
It's essential to ... / I'd recommend -ing
It's essential to stir it; I'd recommend using olive oil.
Avoid + -ing / Be careful not to ...
Avoid taking it out early; be careful not to overcook it.
exceptions: Recommend and avoid are followed by -ing, not an infinitive.
After be careful, use not + infinitive with to.

vocab.example: Talk me through the recipe step by step.
Go over a few basics before you start.
This helps you figure out what they know.
Break the process down into smaller stages.
Don't leave out any important details.
Slow down at the most important points.
Don't go into all the details now.
Use diagrams to get the information across.

reading.summary: An article offers tips for explaining even a simple process: check what the listener knows, divide the task into stages, keep details limited and use creative ways to show meaning.

listening.summary: Sentence practice focusing on stress in phrasal verbs used for explaining.
A YouTuber explains how to make a vegetable lasagne and reveals a secret ingredient.
Extracts practising phrases for stages, necessity and warnings in the lasagne explanation.
Mediation model showing how to make a concept easier for someone else to understand.

speaking: Teach a partner how to do something, using ordered stages, optional stages and warnings about problems.
Predict which parts of your explanation might be difficult and simplify them.
writing: Write a short set of instructions for a simple process, marking essential and optional stages.

practice.q: Could you ... the instructions ... for me, from the beginning?
practice.why: It means to explain something from beginning to end.

practice.q: Let's ... the task ... into smaller stages.
practice.why: It means to separate a process into smaller parts.

practice.q: It's ... to stir the sauce, or it won't be smooth.
practice.why: This marks a stage that is completely necessary.

practice.q: Be careful not to ... any important details.
practice.why: It means to forget or omit something.

lessons.title: Hard work or talent?
goals: Join in a debate about talent and hard work
Use concession words to introduce contrasting ideas

grammar.title: Adverbials of concession
grammar.shortAr: however / though / although / on the other hand لإدخال فكرة معاكسة.
points: However introduces a contrasting sentence and is followed by a comma.
However cannot join two clauses in one sentence with just a comma.
Though or although can join clauses or start a sentence; only though can end a sentence.
On the one hand ... on the other hand presents both sides of an argument.
table: However, ... — contrasting sentence
Talent matters. However, practice is still needed.
clause, though ... — joined clauses
Talent is great, though it is not enough.
Although ..., ... — beginning
Although she is talented, she never practises.
..., though. — end of sentence
The training was hard. It was fun, though.
On the one hand ... on the other hand ...
On the one hand talent helps; on the other hand work develops it.
exceptions: Although cannot come at the end of a sentence; use though instead.
Do not use however to join two clauses with a comma.

vocab.example: You still need some natural talent to help you.
If you put enough hard work in, you will succeed.
You can't get by on talent alone.
Talent helps you excel at a skill.
I'm good at cooking; it runs in my blood.
You must work hard to get anywhere in life.
Talent is a necessary foundation, but not enough.
Drive and passion can take you further than talent.

reading.summary: Street interviews ask speakers whether talent or hard work matters more, and introduce common phrases for discussing natural ability, effort and family talents.

listening.summary: Review listening for the gap-fill text about talent, practice and regrets.

video.summary: Street interviews give different views on whether talent or hard work is more important.

speaking: Discuss three talents you wish you had and how others could use them, conceding and contrasting points.
Say whether someone around you has these talents and what we can learn from them.
writing: Write a social media post giving your view on talent versus hard work.

practice.q: She is very talented, ... she never practises.
practice.why: Though can join two clauses in one sentence.

practice.q: The training was hard. It was enjoyable, ...
practice.why: Only though can end a sentence.

practice.q: ... the weather was bad, we enjoyed the concert.
practice.why: Although introduces a contrasting clause at the beginning.

practice.q: ... the one hand talent helps, but on the other hand practice is vital.
practice.why: The fixed phrase is on the one hand ... on the other hand.

review.summary: Review deduction, regrets, process language and concession while recycling talent vocabulary and idioms.
tasks: Choose the correct past modal for each piece of evidence and speculate about strange scenarios.
Write sentences about your own wishes, regrets and decisions you would change.
Complete a short text with idioms, compound adjectives and explaining phrasal verbs.

quiz.q: He ... have left yet; his bag is still here.
If you'd stayed in that job, you ... have been promoted.
She's been working beside you for months. You ... have met her!
I wish I ... more time to practise the piano.
If only I ... my chance when I was younger!
I ... have given up so early; it was a mistake.
It's essential ... early for the concert.
I'd recommend ... a short break before you continue.
Talent is important, ... hard work is what develops it.

options: a hidden benefit in a bad event
quiz.answer: a hidden benefit in a bad event

quiz.q: What caused Tony Cicoria's sudden love of piano music?
Which reply concedes a point before adding a contrast?
options: I agree, though I still think practice matters.
quiz.answer: I agree, though I still think practice matters.
